report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Timely identification of Barrett's esophagus (BE) is crucial for early esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) detection.
Screening is recommended from age 50 in individuals with additional risk factors, but biological BE onset age remains unknown.
Estimate biological BE onset age and duration before clinical diagnosis (dwell time).
We applied a BE epigenetic clock to 61 samples from 41 patients in a population-representative Northern Ireland cohort and 164 samples from 140 patients in an independent UK cohort.
BE dwell times were compared between patients with concurrent dysplasia/EAC and age-and sex-matched non-dysplastic BE controls in these cross-sectional studies.
In a longitudinal cohort, preprogression biopsies from 31 future high-grade dysplasia (HGD)/EAC progressors were compared with 35 non-progressors.
NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
Median estimated BE onset ages in the cross-sectional cohorts were 29.5 (IQR=22.5-45.8) and 29.3 (IQR=20.4-39.0) years, respectively.
These estimates were further supported by independent epidemiologic modeling of age-specific BE prevalence data from more than 70,000 BE cases.
Estimated dwell times were longer in patients with concurrent dysplasia (median difference 14.3 years; p=0.0042) or EAC (12.5 years; p=0.0002) than matched non-dysplastic BE controls.
Dwell time exceeding 19.8 years was associated with higher odds of HGD/EAC progression (OR=12.1, 95% CI 3.7-47.5; p=9.96 × 10⁻⁵).
BE may arise decades before diagnosis.
Although these findings do not justify lowering screening age, they suggest one-time screening from age 50 years may detect existing high-risk BE.
Further modeling is warranted to evaluate implications for population-based screening, alongside prospective validation of epigenetic tissue age for progression risk stratification.

Increasing patient age is a major clinical risk factor for both esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) and its precursor lesion, Barrett's esophagus (BE), but the biological age or dwell time of BE before diagnosis cannot be directly measured clinically, limiting our understanding of BE onset timing and past disease evolution.
Using a methylation-based molecular clock model applied to 294 tissue samples, we estimated that the median age of onset of BE is approximately 30 years old in 3 independent UK cohorts with BE.

We found substantial interpatient variability in estimated BE onset age, significantly older BE tissue age in patients with adjacent EAC or dysplasia, and 12-fold higher odds of HGD/EAC progression for patients with older BE tissue age in a prospectively followed cohort.

These findings suggest that BE may arise decades before clinical diagnosis, providing a prolonged window for EAC prevention and supporting further investigation of one-time screening from age 50 to identify existing high-risk BE, rather than broadly lowering screening ages.

Molecular estimates of BE tissue age may improve computational models of BE natural history and inform future biomarkers for neoplastic progression risk stratification, warranting further modeling and prospective validation to assess their potential utility in personalized screening and surveillance strategies.

text.text: However, BE onset age has historically been difficult to estimate because metaplastic tissue may persist asymptomatically for decades before diagnosis.
We previously developed a Bayesian molecular clock that uses age-associated DNA methylation drift at selected CpG sites to estimate patient-specific BE onset age and tissue dwell time 28 .

text.text: Here, we applied this molecular clock to three UK study cohorts to characterize BE onset ages and dwell times, including validation against normal gastroesophageal tissues and independent epidemiologic modeling.

We further compared BE tissue ages between age-matched patients with non-dysplastic BE and those with prevalent HGD/EAC and evaluated whether tissue age at initial BE diagnosis was associated with subsequent neoplastic progression in a matched longitudinal case-control cohort.
Together, these analyses aimed to clarify the natural history of BE and assess the potential of molecular tissue age as a biomarker for personalized surveillance.

text.text: In logistic regression analyses adjusting for chronological age at sampling and sex, patients with older BE tissue ages (>19.8 years) had significantly greater odds of subsequent neoplastic progression than those with younger tissue ages (OR = 12.1, 95% CI 3.7-47.5; p=9.96 × 10⁻⁵; Figure 6F).

text.text: Although the wide confidence interval reflects modest cohort size, this finding suggests that BE tissue age exceeding 20 years may represent an important threshold for surveillance risk stratification.

Consistent with this finding, when BE dwell time was modeled as a continuous variable, each 14.2-year increase (equivalent to one standard deviation of BE dwell time among the 66 patients) was associated with nearly 4-fold higher odds of progression (adjusted OR = 3.94, 95% CI: 2.05-8.65).

Taken together, these findings suggest that patients undergoing BE surveillance who are similar in chronological age may nevertheless have substantially different BE tissue ages, as measured using epigenetic data derived from their bulk BE biopsy.

Importantly, these differences were associated with subsequent neoplastic progression, supporting the potential utility of BE tissue age as a molecular biomarker for risk stratification beyond conventional clinical measures.

Barrett's esophagus (BE) is an asymptomatic precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) that is often undetected before cancer diagnosis.
Although the annual risk of progression from nondysplastic BE to EAC is low (0.1-0.3%), the estimated lifetime risk of ~10% 48 is sufficient to explain the overall burden of EAC in the US 16 .

text.text: Reducing EAC mortality depends on first identifying individuals with BE and subsequently detecting and treating high-grade dysplasia (HGD) or early EAC during surveillance.

Current US and European screening guidelines consider age ≥50 years as an established risk factor 10, 12, 23, 24 , yet rising BE incidence rates rising in younger populations 25 who have substantial prevalent neoplasia risk 46 highlights the need to better understand when BE develops and how long it persists before clinical detection.

text.text: We applied an established BE molecular clock to DNA methylation data from 294 total samples across three UK study cohorts to estimate BE onset age and biological tissue age (dwell time).

Model validation using normal gastric cardia, squamous esophagus, and gastroesophageal junction tissues demonstrated minimal epigenetic divergence from the reference normal state, compared with significantly greater dwell times in the BE tissue.
Estimates were further validated using two independent epigenetic clock models.
In the population-based Northern Ireland Barrett's Oesophagus Register (NIBR), we found the median estimated BE onset age was 29.5 years, with 87.5% of patients developing BE before age 50.
Similar results were observed in the Cambridge cohort (median 29.3 years; 87.7% before age 50).
In the independent NIBR-Progressor cohort, median onset age was somewhat higher (37.6 years), although 78.8% of patients still had estimated onset before age 50.
To independently evaluate these estimates, we modeled BE onset using published US age-specific prevalence data.

The fitted population onset-age distribution had a median of 37.9 years, compared with 31.5 years when conditioned on the endoscopy ages of the NIBR cohort, closely matching our methylationbased estimates.
Simulations further demonstrated that median onset age can vary by approximately 10 years across modestly sized cohorts due to age-dependent ascertainment.
These findings suggest that the population median BE onset age may be near 40 years, whereas clinically diagnosed cohorts may have younger median onset ages near 30 years.

This ascertainment effect may also explain the tendency toward later estimated onset in women, who are generally diagnosed at older ages, as sex differences were not significant after matching on age at sampling.
Beyond informing BE natural history, molecular tissue age may provide a biomarker of neoplastic progression risk.
Epidemiologic studies suggest that progression risk accumulates with time since BE diagnosis 27, 49, 50 , potentially reflecting ongoing mutation accumulation and clonal evolution.

text.text: However, biological BE duration may be more informative than time since clinical diagnosis.

Consistent with this hypothesis, BE dwell times were significantly longer in patients with adjacent dysplasia (median difference 14.3 years; p=0.0042) or concurrent EAC (median difference 12.5 years; p=0.00019) compared with matched patients with non-dysplastic BE.

Interestingly, we previously found that patients with a family history of BE/EAC, a known risk factor for EAC progression, also had older BE tissue ages 28 , but were unable to analyze this in the current study populations.

text.text: Moreover, in an age-matched nested case-control cohort, BE tissue age exceeding 19.8 years at initial diagnosis was associated with 12-fold increased odds of subsequent HGD/EAC progression.
Together, these findings suggest that molecular estimates of BE duration may capture clinically relevant variation in progression risk beyond chronological patient age.

Our study has several limitations, including modest sample sizes, although findings were consistent across independent cohorts, tissue preservation methods (archival FFPE and freshfrozen biopsies), and methylation platforms (Illumina EPIC and Twist Human Methylome Panel).
Because BE onset cannot be directly observed histologically, our clock may capture an earlier molecular event preceding metaplasia rather than its precise initiation.
Recent whole-genome sequencing evidence suggests that copy number alterations may arise decades before clinical BE detection 51 , supporting the possibility of early molecular evolution.
text.formatted: Recent whole-genome sequencing evidence suggests that copy number alterations may arise decades before clinical BE detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51</ref> , supporting the possibility of early molecular evolution.

text.text: Nevertheless, the agreement between methylation-based and independent epidemiologic estimates supports the biological plausibility of our inferred onset ages.

Epidemiologic estimates may be affected by misclassification from diagnostic and procedure codes in the largest dataset evaluated, although similar age-specific prevalence trends were observed in two studies requiring histopathologic confirmation of BE.
Residual confounding by BE segment length, BMI, smoking, GERD, or treatment history cannot be excluded because these variables were not consistently available.
Additionally, the absence of spatial sampling information in NIBR and the use of BE tissue adjacent to EAC tumors in Cambridge may introduce heterogeneity given the polyclonal nature of BE.
However, our objective was to estimate the biological age of BE tissue as a potential global marker of accumulated risk, without requiring identification of the specific clone giving rise to cancer.
Our findings suggest that bulk BE biopsies could provide clinically useful information, although larger longitudinal studies with spatial sampling are needed.
An additional consideration is that greater epigenetic aging in BE tissue from progressors may reflect longer dwell times, accelerated methylation drift, or both.
Elevated drift rates could also indicate a broader epigenetic field effect associated with neoplasia.
Although our hierarchical Bayesian model jointly estimates onset age and CpG-specific drift rates, these mechanisms cannot be fully disentangled.

Nevertheless, the independent epidemiologic validation supports the plausibility of inferred onset ages, while the observed differences between progressors and nonprogressors suggest that clock-derived epigenetic aging captures biologically meaningful variation in progression risk.
Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential of methylation-based molecular clocks to reconstruct BE natural history and identify patients at increased risk of neoplastic progression.

More broadly, leveraging passive DNA methylation changes to estimate biological tissue age from relatively low-cost bulk methylation data may provide a broadly applicable biomarker of cancer evolution, with potential to inform risk stratification across diverse precancerous conditions and cancer types 52 .
text.formatted: More broadly, leveraging passive DNA methylation changes to estimate biological tissue age from relatively low-cost bulk methylation data may provide a broadly applicable biomarker of cancer evolution, with potential to inform risk stratification across diverse precancerous conditions and cancer types <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> .

text.text: Estimating when BE develops, often decades before diagnosis, may improve computational models of BE natural history and inform future screening strategies and clinical trial design.
Importantly, these findings do not support broadly lowering screening ages.
Rather, the association between BE tissue age exceeding approximately 20 years and subsequent progression suggests a prolonged window for early detection and intervention.
This raises the possibility that screening beginning at age 50 could identify much of the high-risk BE population before neoplastic progression, warranting further population-based modeling.
The clinical priority is therefore not simply earlier BE detection but identifying those patients most likely to progress to EAC.
Incorporating molecular estimates of BE duration into future risk prediction models could enable more personalized surveillance and timely intervention to prevent EAC.
